title: Structural Traps — Moral Hazard
metadata_mapping: Existing article and responsive illustration conventions; provenance note only, no publication action.

patterns.title: Moral Hazard: Hidden Actions After Agreement

sources.title: Bengt Holmström, Moral Hazard and Observability (1979)
sources.supports: Hidden actions affect outcome distributions; contracting trades incentive provision against risk sharing. Additional information is valuable under the stated model when it adds relevant information about action beyond the payoff.
sources.read_method: Original paper opened and read: introduction and model, printed pp. 74–76, and sufficient-statistic/informativeness discussion on printed p. 84.
sources.boundary: Conditional principal-agent analysis, not measured camera-packing behavior, a universal deductible prescription, or a guarantee that every monitor improves a contract. The camera scenario has separately stipulated qualitative preferences and participation conditions.

sources.title: Willard G. Manning and colleagues, Health Insurance and the Demand for Medical Care: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment (1987)
sources.supports: RAND randomized insurance cost sharing and expenditure limits; lower cost sharing was associated with greater medical spending under the assigned plans.
sources.read_method: Original PDF opened but exposed no readable text through the available web extraction. Study design and direction of the spending result checked against Einav and Finkelstein’s authored review, RAND discussion on printed pp. 966–967; this entry does not claim an independent full-text review of Manning’s methods.
sources.boundary: Historical experiment in its study population and contract designs. Utilization responses do not establish neglect of prevention, dishonesty, that forgone care was wasteful, or the best contract for Tess. No experiment effect size is transferred.

sources.title: Liran Einav and Amy Finkelstein, Moral Hazard in Health Insurance: What We Know and How We Know It (2018)
sources.supports: Distinction between hidden prevention behavior and the broader health-insurance use of moral hazard for healthcare spending responding to out-of-pocket prices; RAND assignment structure and spending direction; limits on extrapolation to unobserved contracts.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted full paper opened and read: abstract/introduction, terminology on printed pp. 959–960, RAND discussion on pp. 966–967, and out-of-sample interpretation on pp. 970–972.
sources.boundary: Specialist review, not a primary experiment for every summarized finding. Observable utilization is distinguished from the camera example’s hidden packing action. Lower spending alone does not establish welfare improvement; extrapolating contract effects requires additional assumptions.

use_when: Post-agreement private actions can affect losses while the actor does not bear all their consequences.
A claim rate or damaged item is being treated as proof of carelessness without evidence about behavior or baseline risk.
goals: Distinguish hidden action after agreement from private characteristics affecting entry.
Separate prevention incentives, uncontrollable damage, participation, risk bearing, and welfare.
Distinguish the camera benchmark from broader healthcare terminology and utilization evidence.
mechanisms: Reconnect some preventable loss to the private choice where affordable and action-changing.
Use informative observation or make prevention easier.
Count the risk shifted to the renter and verify participation.

example_structure.scenario: Tess privately chooses extra camera packing after accepting a full damage waiver. Care reduces damage probability, costs effort, and is not fully observed. One-rental own-material benchmark excludes future reputation.
example_structure.changed_relationship: A proposed deductible changes the private benefit of prevention; more care follows only when avoided private loss outweighs effort and Tess still prefers renting.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Good packing does not rule out damage. Tess may bear more risk and be worse off. If she cannot influence the risk, a deductible adds exposure without the intended prevention.
example_structure.evidence: Hypothetical choice and stipulated continuation, not a measured outcome. No illustrative calculation is required.

visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Under full financial protection, Tess bears packing effort but the pool pays the covered repair loss. Under the proposed deductible Tess still bears effort and also the initial part of a covered loss; the pool bears the remainder. Packing stays private and damage stays uncertain. More care is conditional on the private loss reduction outweighing effort. Change: Reconnect preventable loss to the decision, or reduce prevention effort directly. Limitation: More care is conditional on incentives and acceptable terms. Tess may bear more risk and be worse off.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. Compare the same two burdens before and after the deductible. Effort never moves away from Tess; part of the financial loss moves toward her. This can change prevention incentives while increasing her risk, and good packing cannot rule out damage.

representation.relationship_key: Rows allocate effort and financial loss. Lower arrows show private action preceding an uncertain outcome.
representation.changed_relationship: A deductible moves an initial share of covered financial loss toward Tess while packing effort stays with her.
representation.residual_constraints: Action stays private and damage remains uncertain; incentive improvement does not establish a better overall contract.

patterns.evidence_boundary: A new provenance note for the existing article; no article, source claim, illustration, or publication status changed. Reading performed on 2 November 2026 is recorded precisely; unavailable original-paper text is distinguished from review-based corroboration.
